metric_rationale: This high-conflict cue-dominance index uses only trials on which the first discriminating cue and the equal-weight tally make opposite predictions, with tally supported by at least a three-vote net margin. TTB predicts that the top-cue option will nevertheless win a majority of the 64 selected trials, whereas Tallying predicts the opposite. Pooling across many repetitions and A/B reversals makes the majority classification resistant to trial noise and response-side bias. The threshold yields a readily interpretable scalar—whether strong lower-cue majorities overturn the validity-ranked cue—and should produce values near 1 under TTB and near 0 under Tallying while remaining defined on each subject separately.

This metric makes a bounded model-selection decision rather than measuring an unstable effect magnitude. It compares the best exact Tallying reliability curve across margins 1–6 with TTB's margin-invariant reliability and applies the standard AIC penalty for Tallying's additional identifiable shape parameter. The output is 1 only when the observed gain in fit exceeds that complexity cost. Consequently, occasional noisy margin contrasts do not produce arbitrarily large subject-level values, and the between-subject variance is bounded by 0.25. The criterion is not guaranteed by Tallying: weak, highly lapsed, or noisy tally-generated data can select TTB, while sufficiently systematic human increases in choice reliability with tally margin select Tallying.

This is a preregistered high-consistency exceedance indicator: it asks whether at least 90% of choices agree with the option favored by the first discriminating cue. It is not logically guaranteed by either theory because both include response noise and lapses. Under the advocated TTB parameter range, broad heterogeneity in beta and lapse rate yields pooled first-cue consistency substantially below 90%. The competing cascade uses beta between 4 and 16, lapses no greater than 0.15, and all six cues exceed its stopping threshold; it should therefore exceed 90% consistency despite weaker evidence at later cue ranks. Dichotomizing at a threshold lying between these predictions produces a large canonical separation, while 96 repeated trials make each subject's classification reasonably stable. The metric remains well-defined on both pooled data and single-subject slices.

This metric measures the central qualitative reversal rather than the comparatively small centered gradient used by the failed metric. At conflict levels 2–6, the aggregate of the equally valid weak cues points opposite to Expert 2. Confidence-Capped Cascade Integration therefore favors the aggregate winner, with strength generally increasing across those levels. Take The Best always follows Expert 2, so it chooses the metric-defined winner only through response noise or lapses. Pooling all five reversal levels supplies 80 observations per subject, reducing binomial variability, while exact A/B reversals cancel response-side bias. The expected contrast is consequently a large difference in overall reversal rate rather than a small difference between noisy condition means.

This is the strong-conflict majority-override rate, pooled across conflict levels 5 and 6 and their exact A/B reversals. It measures a psychologically interpretable event: choosing the option supported by a large coalition of slightly less valid cues even though the single more-valid 72% cue recommends the other option. TTB should produce a low rate because it stops at the 72% cue and never consults the 70% cues. Priority Race Search should produce a high rate because, at these conflict levels, at least one earlier-displayed 70% cue has a parameter-robust priority advantage and normally wins the stopping-cue race. Restricting the contrast to the two strongest levels preserves that robust separation, while combining 32 trials per subject and balancing choice side through exact reversals reduces sampling variance and response-side bias.

This endpoint crossover contrast subtracts the probability of following the higher-validity cue at the smallest validity-log-odds gap from that probability at the largest gap. It pools each trial with its exact A/B reversal, so response-side preferences are balanced, and it uses 16 observations at each endpoint per subject. Take The Best predicts the same probability of following the higher-validity cue at both endpoints, making the expected contrast zero even when its response-noise parameters vary across subjects. Noisy Priority Race Search predicts a large positive contrast: the two-position serial advantage makes the earlier, slightly less valid cue likely to win at the smallest gap, whereas the large validity advantage dominates serial priority and representation bias at the largest gap. Restricting the statistic to the two parameter-robust endpoints avoids the additional between-subject crossover-location variance present in intermediate conditions.

This is a centered matched-filter contrast for the shape uniquely at issue in the design. Each response is recoded as choosing the option supported by the designated high-validity target cue, thereby combining A/B-reversed versions and suppressing response-side bias. Positive weights are assigned to early target positions and negative weights to late positions, with magnitudes approximating the competing cascade's predicted accessibility profile. Because the weights sum to zero and every condition is equally repeated, Take The Best's position-invariant target-choice probability predicts a metric near zero for every beta and epsilon. The accessibility-gated cascade predicts a large positive value because target-following choices decline sharply with display position. Using all six positions and all 96 trials should yield substantially lower per-subject sampling variance than an endpoint-only early-minus-late contrast.

This is an extreme-groups redundancy gain: the increase in following the 95%-valid cue when it is supported by five or six same-direction terminal cues rather than only one or two. TTB predicts an expected value of zero because the 95% cue is already the first discriminating cue in every condition; its beta and lapse parameters affect both groups equally. The accessibility-gated cascade predicts a large positive value because additional terminal cues rescue decisions when still-higher-validity terminal cues are inaccessible. Pooling two conditions at each extreme gives 32 observations per group per subject, reducing binomial variance, while coding choices relative to the top cue and combining exact A/B reversals cancels response-side bias. Intermediate conditions are omitted because the endpoint regions provide a larger predicted contrast per unit of trial noise.

This is the within-subject increase in following the uniquely highest-validity cue when its six redundant supporters are sparse (mean offsets 7 or 10) rather than dense/intermediate (offsets 2–5). Take The Best predicts the same probability of following Expert 17 in every arrangement, so its expected contrast is zero even when beta, lapse rate, or overall response accuracy differ across subjects. The competing cascade predicts substantially greater congruence in sparse displays because reduced source competition restores retrieval of Expert 17 or another same-direction high-validity cue. Pooling 32 sparse and 64 dense observations per subject yields a stable estimate, while coding choices relative to Expert 17 and including exact A/B reversals cancels fixed response-side preferences.

This is the terminal-cluster recovery contrast: the rate of choosing the option supported by the adjacent 82%-valid cue pair at positions 31–32 minus the corresponding rate pooled across positions 1–2 through 25–26. Scoring choices relative to the cluster, rather than as raw A choices, combines the exact A/B reversals and removes response-side preference. Pooling all five nonterminal locations provides 80 comparison trials per subject while retaining 16 terminal trials, reducing sampling variance. Take The Best predicts the same cluster-following probability at every location, so its expected contrast is zero for every parameter setting. The Competitive Source-Binding Cascade predicts a sizable positive contrast because the terminal pair receives both the long-display positional advantage and the sharply localized recency boost. This is a substantive behavioral interaction with display position rather than a direct restatement of an internal model quantity.

This is an extreme-condition redundancy contrast: the probability of choosing the option supported by the 82%-valid sources with 6–7 such sources minus the corresponding probability with 2–3 sources. Responses are recoded relative to the evidence-supported option, so the exact A/B reversals cancel response-side preferences. The advocated source-based interference and shared-gate account predicts a strongly negative contrast because large redundant sets overload retrieval. The competing spatial-competition cascade predicts a positive contrast because the widely separated sources remain relatively independent and provide additional chances to stop the cascade before the opposing 70%-valid source. Pooling adjacent endpoint conditions retains 64 trials per subject, reducing binomial variance while avoiding the less diagnostic middle of the predicted nonlinear transition.

The metric is the increase in choices following the 82%-valid target when it appears at the terminal position versus the three early target positions. It pools both A/B reversals by scoring agreement with the target cue, thereby canceling response-side effects. The advocated binding cascade predicts a large positive contrast because its localized recency boost is negligible at positions 14–18 but maximal at position 24. The competing retrieval theory predicts a contrast near zero or slightly negative because isolated cues have no recency benefit and only a weak late-position loss. Averaging 48 early-position observations against 16 terminal observations per subject keeps binomial variance substantially lower than a single endpoint-to-endpoint contrast while retaining most of the predicted recency separation.

This metric is the run-length-weighted embedded-anchor advantage: the probability of choosing the option supported by the contiguous expert run when its uniquely strongest expert is interior, minus the corresponding probability when that expert is at the boundary. Choices are recoded relative to the run-supported option, so exact A/B reversals cancel response-side biases. The advocated source-based chunking theory predicts approximately zero contrast at every length because each matched pair has the same validity multiset, source load, and chunk priority. The competing structure-gated theory predicts a positive contrast because interior anchors receive a 90% reduction in overload, with the effect increasing from length 3 to length 5. Weighting longer runs more heavily targets that predicted growth while retaining all three independent matched contrasts to reduce trial-level noise. The statistic remains directly computable and stable on each subject's 96-trial slice.

The metric is the adjacency effect on choosing the option supported by the two equally valid 82% experts, after recoding the A/B reversals so positive values always indicate an adjacency advantage. It derives condition and supported option directly from each stimulus rather than relying on randomized trial order. Structure-Gated Ensemble Lexicographic Retrieval predicts a positive effect because an adjacent pair receives a high-fidelity representation, whereas the competing theory predicts a negative effect because separated sources provide two retrieval opportunities while an adjacent chunk usually provides one. Each subject contributes 48 adjacent and 48 separated observations, so the within-subject difference removes general pair-choice and response-side biases while retaining low sampling variance.

The metric is the within-subject drop in choosing the fixed six-expert run-supported option when the opposing recommendation changes from one supporter to multiple supporters. It first recodes the exact A/B reversals into a common run-choice outcome, eliminating response-side preference, then contrasts the 16 observations with one opponent (two orientations × eight repetitions) against the 80 observations with two through six opponents. Competition-Normalized Recommendation Race predicts a large positive value because its overload gate switches on at the second opposing supporter and then saturates. Structure-Gated Ensemble Lexicographic Retrieval predicts a value near zero because the run representation is already overloaded in every condition and separated opposing sources receive only a negligible count gain. Pooling all post-gate conditions both captures the sustained cliff and substantially lowers per-subject sampling variance; the within-subject contrast also cancels stable differences in lapse rate and overall propensity to follow the run.

This is the orientation-invariant two-pairs advantage among the four-source trials: the probability of choosing the option supported by two separated adjacent pairs minus the probability of choosing the option supported by one contiguous run of four. It pools each condition with its exact A/B reversal, cancelling response-side bias, and uses 16 observations per condition per subject. The advocated theory predicts a large positive contrast because two high-fidelity pair chunks provide separate retrieval opportunities, whereas a length-four run suffers substantial overload. The competing theory predicts essentially zero because it compresses all four supporters into one recommendation and its run-overload gate is inactive against a singleton opponent. Restricting the metric to the strongest predicted structural contrast avoids diluting it with the smaller three-source effect.

This is the within-subject opponent-count effect at the maximally diagnostic run length. Competition-Normalized Recommendation Race predicts that a six-source contiguous run is largely unpenalized against a singleton, but incurs a large density-overload cost when the opponent has two supporters. It therefore predicts a sizable positive difference. The competing theory assigns the six-source recommendation essentially the same intrinsic capacity cost in both conditions, so it predicts a difference near zero. Restricting the metric to the six-source trials avoids diluting the contrast with the theoretically null three-source cells, while coding choices relative to the run-supported option combines exact A/B reversals and cancels response-side tendencies. Each subject contributes 16 trials to each term, yielding a stable within-subject contrast.

The metric is the reversal-balanced probability of choosing the recommendation supported by all six 94%-valid experts against the fixed 70%-valid singleton. This is the design's largest predicted separation: intrinsic recommendation capacity sharply reduces retrieval of the six-source 94% recommendation under the advocated theory, whereas the competing theory has neither density overload (the sources are separated and face a singleton) nor a meaningful count effect. Restricting the metric to this high-effect condition avoids adding sampling noise from the nearly nondiagnostic 80% and smaller-count cells. Exact A/B reversals make the following rate insensitive to a stable response-side preference, and each subject contributes 16 trials, yielding a stable subject-level estimate.

This side-invariant extreme-condition contrast measures the increase in choosing the six-expert bundle when its supporters move from highly homogeneous to strongly heterogeneous validities. It pools the two most homogeneous and two most heterogeneous conditions, including their A/B reversals and repetitions, to reduce per-subject sampling variance. Causal-copy discounting predicts a large positive difference because homogeneous agreement is severely discounted while heterogeneous agreement is not. The competing theory uses the same strongest expert and source count in every condition, so it predicts a contrast near zero. Intermediate conditions are omitted because they dilute the theoretically sharp nonlinear separation.

The metric is the proportion of trials on which the subject follows the 82%-valid target recommendation rather than the opposing 80%-valid singleton, pooling all singleton/pair locations and exact A/B reversals. The advocated theory predicts appreciably greater target following: its recommendation-level competition and strong late-position accessibility gain make the 82% target highly retrievable, whereas the competing theory's local priority mixing permits the 80% recommendation to govern a meaningful fraction of these near-tie choices and provides no positive late-position gain. Pooling all 96 trials exploits both the broad quantitative target-following difference and the advocated theory's singleton position effect while sharply reducing per-subject binomial variance. Exact reversals ensure that the score is not a response-side preference. This is not a definitional consequence of either theory: both rank 82% above 80%, but they make different quantitative predictions about how reliably that ranking controls choice.
